docs.title: Welcome to Bumper 🤖
docs.text:
Bumper is a local replacement for Ecovacs cloud services, allowing your robots and apps to connect entirely within your home network - without needing access to the original cloud.

It supports both XMPP and MQTT-based models transparently.

Disclaimer: This project is a work in progress and may contain errors or missing parts. Please refer to the documentation and source code for complete details.

docs.title: ⚙️ Requirements
docs.text:
• A Wi-Fi enabled Ecovacs robot
  • A server in your local network to run the Bumper services
  • Python 3.13 or newer (3.15 recommended) with uv or Docker
  • A DNS server capable of overriding specific domain queries
  • A client that can connect and control the robot:
    • The official "Ecovacs" or "Ecovacs Home" Android/iOS apps (when configured correctly)
      • See Using Bumper with the official App for mobile setup details.
    • DeebotUniverse/client.py for command-line control

docs.title: 1. 🤖 Prepare your Robot
docs.text: • Set up your robot using the official Ecovacs app (initial Wi-Fi configuration, registration, etc.)

docs.title: 2. 🌐 Set up DNS
docs.text:
• Configure your local DNS server to override specific Ecovacs domains.
  • Detailed setup instructions: DNS Setup

docs.title: 3. 🛠️ Install and Run Bumper
docs.text: • Follow the installation and usage instructions in the README.md or refer to Docker Setup if using Docker.

docs.title: 4. 🔒 Certificates
docs.text:
• Bumper requires valid certificates to operate.
  • Instructions for manually creating certificates are available here: Create Certificates

docs.title: 📋 Logs and Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Bumper writes log files into the /logs directory by default. You can also monitor real-time output:

  • If running manually: logs appear directly in the terminal.
  • If running via Docker: use docker logs <container-name> to view logs.

For more detailed output and debugging:

  • Additional debugging can be enabled using environment variables. See Environment Variables for a list of available debug options.

docs.title: Bumper Origins & Maintenance
docs.text:
The Bumper project was originally created by @torbjornaxelsson in 2017 as a reverse engineering tool to interface with certain EcoVacs robotic vacuums. It successfully reached its initial goal and remained in a stable (but no longer actively maintained) state, with the last update committed in December 2017.

In early 2019, @bmartin5692 picked up the project to support newer vacuum models that use updated protocols. His fork introduced key changes and improvements to the original codebase and continued development for several years.

Later, @edenhaus forked the project to refactor and modernize large portions of the codebase, aiming to clean up architectural issues, enhance maintainability, and support more recent devices. This fork has since diverged significantly and is now actively maintained as the primary development source going forward.

docs.title: 🔧 Current Maintenance
docs.text:
This repository is now the actively maintained version of Bumper. It includes:

  • Major refactors for stability and code clarity
  • Updated support for newer EcoVacs models and protocols
  • Improved documentation
  • Better compatibility with modern environments

docs.title: 📦 Legacy Versions
docs.text:
If you're looking for the older versions:

  • The original 2017 codebase by @torbjornaxelsson is archived.
  • The intermediate development fork by @bmartin5692 is still available.
  • A historical snapshot of the pre-refactor code is preserved as v0.1.0 in his fork.

⚠️ That legacy version may still work with some early models (e.g. M81 Pro, N79S), but for all current and future use, this repository is recommended.

docs.title: Environment Variables Overview
docs.text: Bumper's behavior can be tailored by setting environment variables before startup. Below is a list of all variables that the Python application reads, grouped by category. Variables not listed here are hardcoded or not configurable via environment.

docs.title: ⏰ Timezone
docs.text: Variable Default Description TZ UTC Timezone for scheduling and log timestamps. Set to any IANA zone, e.g., Europe/Berlin. SYNC_TIMEZONE false Sync the server timezone offset to robots when they connect over MQTT.

docs.title: ⚙️ Feature Flags
docs.text: Variable Default Description CA_CERT_API_ONLY_BUMPER_CERT false If true, only the self-signed Bumper CA is served. If false, the bundle also carries the original system CA. USER_USERNAME_DEFAULT bumper Username the local account is presented with. USER_NICKNAME_DEFAULT USER_USERNAME_DEFAULT Display name of the local account. Shown as the member name in the app. USER_MAIL_DEFAULT ${USER_USERNAME_DEFAULT}@home.local Mail address the local account is presented with. PHOTO_MAX_PER_DEVICE 20 How many uploaded files are kept per robot, pictures and cleaned maps alike. The oldest are dropped on every new upload. CLEAN_LOG_MAX_PER_DEVICE 100 How many clean log entries are kept per robot. The oldest are dropped on every new one. WEBVIEW_TRUSTED_HOST_SUFFIXES ecovacs.com,ecovacs.cn,ecouser.net,... Hosts the app may open in a webview. The app ships the Ecovacs domains as a fallback, add the host this instance is reached under.

docs.title: 📁 Paths & Files
docs.text: Variable Default Description BUMPER_DATA $PWD/data Directory for persistent data, uploads and caches. DB_FILE ${BUMPER_DATA}/bumper.db TinyDB database file. The file holds JSON, not SQL. BUMPER_ACCOUNT_KEY ${BUMPER_DATA}/account.key RSA key used to decrypt account fields the app encrypts. Mode 0600. BUMPER_CERTS $PWD/certs Directory for TLS certificate files. BUMPER_VOICES ${BUMPER_DATA}/voices Directory for the voice files the robot downloads. BUMPER_CODEPUSH ${BUMPER_DATA}/codepush Directory for the CodePush packages the app downloads. BUMPER_CA_CERT ${BUMPER_CERTS}/ca.crt Path to the CA certificate. BUMPER_CA is accepted as a deprecated alias. BUMPER_CA_KEY ${BUMPER_CERTS}/ca.key Path to the CA private key. BUMPER_CA_PEM ${BUMPER_CERTS}/ca.pem Path to the combined server key, server certificate and CA certificate. BUMPER_CERT ${BUMPER_CERTS}/bumper.crt Path to the server certificate. BUMPER_KEY ${BUMPER_CERTS}/bumper.key Path to the server private key.

docs.title: 🔐 Certificates
docs.text: Variable Default Description BUMPER_CA_VALID_DAYS 6669 CA certificate validity in days (about 18 years). Long duration for home-hosted self-signed stability. BUMPER_VALID_DAYS 666 Server certificate validity in days (about 22 months). Practical rotation cycle for home management. CERT_KEY_TYPE ec Key algorithm. Accepts only ec (P-256 elliptic curve) or rsa. CERT_RSA_KEY_SIZE 2048 RSA key size in bits. Must be 2048 to 4096. Ignored for EC keys.

docs.title: 🔒 Authentication
docs.text:
Variable Default Description TOKEN_VALIDITY_SECONDS 2592000 Portal-token session lifetime in seconds (30 days). ACCESS_TOKEN_VALIDITY_SECONDS 1800 OAuth access JWT lifetime in seconds (30 minutes). REFRESH_TOKEN_VALIDITY_SECONDS 2592000 OAuth refresh JWT lifetime in seconds (30 days). TOKEN_JWT_ALG Follows key type Algorithm used to sign app tokens. Defaults to ES256 for EC keys and RS256 for RSA keys.

Bumper does not verify Ecovacs request signatures. See Authentication for the full flow.

docs.title: 🌐 Networking
docs.text: Variable Default Description BUMPER_LISTEN Auto-detected via system DNS IP address or hostname to bind all server listeners (Web, MQTT, XMPP). BUMPER_ANNOUNCE_IP ${BUMPER_LISTEN} IP advertised to robots. If 0.0.0.0, set explicitly. WEB_SERVER_HTTPS_PORT 443 Port for the HTTPS web UI and API. WEB_SERVER_LISTEN_PORT 8007 Port for the plain HTTP web UI and API. MQTT_LISTEN_PORT 1883 Plain MQTT listener. MQTT_LISTEN_PORT_TLS 8883 TLS MQTT listener. XMPP_LISTEN_PORT_TLS 5223 TLS XMPP listener. HELPER_BOT_TIMEOUT 10 Seconds the helper bot waits for a robot to answer. The app gives up on a request after 15 seconds, so a longer wait is never seen by it. CODEPUSH_LOCAL_PACKAGE false Serve the CodePush package from this server instead of the cloud. The app then downloads it from the host of the CodePush service, which has to be one that the DNS override points at Bumper.

docs.title: 🚦 Logging & Debugging
docs.text: Variable Default Description DEBUG_BUMPER_LEVEL INFO Log level (NOTSET, DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL). DEBUG_BUMPER_VERBOSE 1 Verbose output per log line (integer 0, 1, 2). DEBUG_LOGGING_API_REQUEST false Log incoming API requests. DEBUG_LOGGING_API_REQUEST_MISSING false Log requests that no route matches. DEBUG_LOGGING_XMPP_REQUEST false Log XMPP requests before internal changes. DEBUG_LOGGING_XMPP_REQUEST_REFACTOR false Log XMPP requests after internal changes. DEBUG_LOGGING_XMPP_RESPONSE false Log XMPP server responses. DEBUG_LOGGING_SA_RESULT false Log service-autonomy outputs from API requests by /sa.

docs.title: 🔗 Proxy & Forwarding
docs.text: Variable Default Description BUMPER_PROXY_MQTT false Forward MQTT traffic to the Ecovacs cloud. BUMPER_PROXY_WEB false Forward web traffic to the Ecovacs cloud. PROXY_PUBLISH_TIMEOUT 10 Seconds a proxied MQTT publish may wait before it is reported as timed out.

docs.title: 🚢 Docker Compose & Swarm Variables
docs.text:
These additional environment variables are used in the compose files to control service deployment and container behavior.

Variable Default Description NODE_ROLE manager Docker Swarm role constraint for service placement (manager or worker). NETWORK_MODE bridge Docker network driver (bridge or overlay). RESOURCES_LIMITS_CPUS 0.25 CPU limit per container. RESOURCES_LIMITS_MEMORY 250m Memory limit per container. RESOURCES_RESERVATIONS_CPUS 0.001 CPU reservation per container. RESOURCES_RESERVATIONS_MEMORY 32m Memory reservation per container. VERSION_BUMPER latest Bumper image tag to deploy. The image reports its build version under the same name. VERSION_NGNIX 1.29-alpine3.22-slim NGINX image tag for the reverse proxy. TZ Europe/Berlin Timezone inside containers (binds to host timezone). docs.title: Development Guide
docs.text: This guide covers setting up a local development environment, running the application, and maintaining code quality.

docs.title: 🔧 Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.15 recommended (3.13 and 3.14 are supported)
  • Git

docs.title: 🛠️ Setup Local Environment
docs.text:
Step 1 - Clone the repository

git clone https://github.com/MVladislav/bumper.git
cd bumper

Step 2 - Create and activate a virtual environment

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

Step 3 - Install uv inside the virtual environment

python3 -m pip install uv

Step 4 - Install project dependencies

uv sync --active --python 3.15 --all-groups --upgrade

docs.title: 🚀 Running the Application
docs.text:
./scripts/certs/create-cert.sh
WEB_SERVER_HTTPS_PORT=8443 uv run --active bumper

The web UI will be available at https://127.0.1.1:8443 by default.

docs.title: Linting & Static Analysis
docs.text:
Run prek hooks

prek run --all-files

Type checking with mypy

uv run --active --frozen mypy bumper/

Linting with pylint

uv run --active --frozen pylint bumper/

docs.title: Unit Tests
docs.text:
Run tests

uv run --active pytest tests

Tests with coverage report

uv run --active pytest --cov=./ tests --cov-report xml --junitxml=pytest-report.xml

Generate HTML coverage report

uv run --active pytest --cov=./ tests --cov-report html:tests/report

The HTML report is located at tests/report/index.html.

  2. Follow the setup and testing steps above.
  3. Commit changes with clear messages and update tests.

See CONTRIBUTING.md for detailed contribution guidelines.

docs.title: Static Data Update Guide
docs.text:
Bumper serves some data from pre-fetched files under bumper/web/static_api/ instead of querying the Ecovacs cloud, so the app keeps working fully offline. This data changes over time; this guide explains which files exist and how to refresh them with the helper scripts in scripts/.

Note: the process is not fully automatable. update-eco-data.sh requires an Ecovacs account login, and the first login from a new device may require an email verification code. The scripts are meant to be run manually by a maintainer.

docs.title: 📦 What Gets Updated
docs.text:
All files live in bumper/web/static_api/ and are served to the app from Bumper's own web server instead of the Ecovacs cloud:

File Served to the app at What it contains configGroupsResponse.json POST /product/getConfigGroups Product groups with their robot models and Wi-Fi setup steps (product configuration screens) configNetAllResponse.json POST /product/getConfignetAll All robot models with their Wi-Fi setup steps (steps, customSteps) productIotMap.json POST /product/getProductIotMap classid → product info (QR-code decoding, bot list enrichment) updateCheck.json GET /v0.1/public/codepush/update_check deployment_key → latest bundle info (download_url, is_available, is_mandatory, …) updateCheck_mapping.json (lookup for the codepush update check) main_folder → deployment_key, resolves update checks sent by package name timezones.json GET /basis/time/timezones The time zones of the app, with their name in every language voices.json GET /pim/voice/get The voice of every language the app offers, with the file the robot has to download

docs.title: 🔄 Scripts
docs.text:
Script Needs login Reads Writes update-eco-data.sh ✅ (password + optional email code) Ecovacs private API configGroupsResponse.json, configNetAllResponse.json, productIotMap.json 1-update-eco-codepush.sh ❌ codePushConfig.json updateCheck.json 2-update-eco-codepush-mapping.sh ❌ updateCheck.json updateCheck_mapping.json 3-update-eco-codepush-packages.sh ❌ updateCheck.json the CodePush packages in the CodePush directory update-eco-timezones.sh ✅ (password + optional email code) Ecovacs api base timezones.json update-eco-voices.sh ✅ (password + optional email code) Ecovacs portal API voices.json and the voice files in the voice directory

Most of the scripts are maintenance: they refresh the information Bumper serves, and the result is pushed into the repository. Run them when that information has to be brought up to date.

Two of them fetch files that are large and that stay out of the repository - the voice files and the CodePush packages. They are only needed when those files are to be served from Bumper instead of from the cloud.

The three CodePush scripts carry a prefix that matches their order inside the group. Run the scripts in this order when you refresh everything. Inside the CodePush group each script needs the output of the previous one; the other scripts are independent.

  1. scripts/data/update-eco-data.sh - logs in to the Ecovacs private API and downloads the per-country product configs (DE, US, other countries from COUNTRIES), combines them with the committed files and rewrites the download URLs to local domains (see combination rules).
  2. scripts/data/1-update-eco-codepush.sh - queries the public codepush update_check endpoint for every deployment key in codePushConfig.json and combines the results into updateCheck.json. Download URLs are stripped of their AWS signing parameters. Downloads run in parallel (ECO_PARALLEL).
  3. scripts/data/2-update-eco-codepush-mapping.sh - downloads the codepush bundles referenced by updateCheck.json, extracts the main folder of each bundle and writes the {main_folder: deployment_key} mapping used by the app (see appsvr.py get_codepush_update_check_data).
  4. scripts/data/3-update-eco-codepush-packages.sh - downloads the CodePush packages of the deployments, so that the app can update without reaching the cloud. Only needed when the packages are to be served from Bumper (CODEPUSH_LOCAL_PACKAGE). The packages are a few MB to a few dozen MB each and are not part of the repository: they land in the CodePush directory (BUMPER_CODEPUSH, ${BUMPER_DATA}/codepush by default). The script needs no login, but it needs the urls of updateCheck.json, so it runs after 1-update-eco-codepush.sh. Downloads run in parallel (ECO_PARALLEL).
  5. scripts/data/update-eco-timezones.sh - fetches the time zones the app shows, with their name in every language, and writes them to timezones.json.
  6. scripts/data/update-eco-voices.sh - fetches the voice of every language the app offers and writes the metadata to voices.json. Only needed when the robot is to change its voice language. The voice files themselves are a few MB each and are not part of the repository: they land in the voice directory (BUMPER_VOICES, ${BUMPER_DATA}/voices by default) and have to be present before the server starts.

All scripts write their per-run artefacts to json_mappings/ (gitignored) and copy the final files into bumper/web/static_api/. All outputs are sorted, so re-runs produce stable diffs.

Note: run the scripts before the DNS override is in place, or from a machine that can still reach the Ecovacs cloud - the override points the cloud names at Bumper.

Note: the voice files and the CodePush packages are the exceptions to "everything ends up in static_api/". They are large and they are fetched from the cloud, so they are kept out of the repository on purpose.

docs.title: 🚀 Usage
docs.text:
Step 1 - Refresh the product data (needs an Ecovacs account):

ECOVACS_ACCOUNT_ID=your@email.com ECOVACS_PASSWORD=your_password scripts/data/update-eco-data.sh

On the first login from a new device, Ecovacs answers with error 1013 and the script triggers a device verification: a code is emailed to the account address and you are prompted for it.

Note: verification codes are single-use and repeated requests are rate-limited by Ecovacs (0002 "Parameter error. Please try again later."). Wait 10-30 minutes before retrying.

Verification is bound to the device id stored in .eco-device-id (gitignored), so subsequent runs log in directly without a code.

Step 2 - Refresh the codepush data (no login needed):

scripts/data/1-update-eco-codepush.sh
scripts/data/2-update-eco-codepush-mapping.sh

Step 3 - Download the CodePush packages (no login needed):

scripts/data/3-update-eco-codepush-packages.sh

Only needed when the packages are to be served from Bumper (CODEPUSH_LOCAL_PACKAGE=true). The script downloads the package of every deployment of updateCheck.json, at the same time. The packages are large, so the deployments to fetch can be named:

CODEPUSH_DEPLOYMENT_KEYS=<the deployment key> scripts/data/3-update-eco-codepush-packages.sh

The files are written to ${BUMPER_DATA}/codepush unless BUMPER_CODEPUSH says otherwise. In a container the data directory is a volume, so the packages either live in that volume or are copied into it:

docker cp ./data/codepush/. <container>:/bumper/data/codepush/

Step 4 - Refresh the time zones (needs an Ecovacs account):

ECOVACS_ACCOUNT_ID=your@email.com ECOVACS_PASSWORD=your_password scripts/data/update-eco-timezones.sh

The time zones are the same for every user, but the api wants a login. The host of the api belongs to the region of the account, API_BASE_HOST sets it.

Step 5 - Refresh the voice files (needs an Ecovacs account):

ECOVACS_ACCOUNT_ID=your@email.com ECOVACS_PASSWORD=your_password scripts/data/update-eco-voices.sh

Only needed when the robot is to change its voice language.

Note: verification codes are single-use and repeated requests are rate-limited by Ecovacs (0002 "Parameter error. Please try again later."). Wait 10-30 minutes before retrying.

Verification is bound to the device id stored in .eco-device-id (gitignored), so subsequent runs log in directly without a code.

The files are written to ${BUMPER_DATA}/voices unless BUMPER_VOICES says otherwise, and the metadata to bumper/web/static_api/voices.json.

In a container the data directory is a volume, so the files either live in that volume or are copied into it:

docker cp ./data/voices/. <container>:/bumper/data/voices/

The app downloads the package from the cloud unless CODEPUSH_DOWNLOAD_HOST names the host that answers for Bumper:

CODEPUSH_DOWNLOAD_HOST=codepush-base.ecouser.net

With that set, the update check answers with the url of the package on that host, and the app downloads it from Bumper instead of from the cloud. The host has to be one that the DNS override points at Bumper.

docs.title: 🔀 Combination Rules
docs.text:
update-eco-data.sh combines the per-country responses with the currently committed files:

  • Country priority: each entry (by id / groupId / classid) is taken from DE if present, otherwise US, otherwise any other country; entries that no country supplies anymore are kept from the committed file.
  • Consistency: object keys are sorted recursively, so key reordering in upstream responses does not produce noisy diffs between runs.
  • Robustness: countries whose request failed are skipped instead of poisoning the combination.

docs.title: ⚙️ Environment Variables
docs.text: Variable Used by Purpose ECOVACS_ACCOUNT_ID, ECOVACS_PASSWORD update-eco-data.sh, update-eco-voices.sh Ecovacs account credentials (required) ECO_DEVICE_ID update-eco-data.sh, update-eco-voices.sh Stable device id (default: generated once and stored in .eco-device-id) ECO_DEVICE_ID_FILE update-eco-data.sh, update-eco-voices.sh Custom path for the device id file ECO_VERIFY_CODE update-eco-data.sh, update-eco-voices.sh Skip the prompt with a pre-fetched email verification code ECO_CHANNEL update-eco-data.sh App channel (google_play default; google worked in some regions) ECO_PARALLEL 1-update-eco-codepush.sh, 2-update-eco-codepush-mapping.sh Number of parallel downloads (default 4) BUMPER_VOICES update-eco-voices.sh Where the voice files are written (default: ${BUMPER_DATA}/voices) VOICE_LANGS update-eco-voices.sh The languages to fetch, comma separated (default: every language) API_BASE_HOST update-eco-timezones.sh The api host of the region (default: api-base.dc-eu.ww.ecouser.net)

docs.title: Web API Endpoints
docs.text: This guide explains how a web route chooses its response shape, how @bind applies that shape, and which response template to start with when adding an endpoint. The route must preserve the exact JSON keys, value types, and failure shape expected by its client.

docs.title: 🧭 The pieces
docs.text:
Piece Job web.RouteTableDef Registers paths and HTTP methods in one plugin module. Route handler Reads the request, performs the operation, and returns the payload. Template Describes the success envelope and its corresponding ErrorShape. @bind(template) Converts a handler's payload or ApiError into the endpoint's response shape. TypedDict payload Names the fields and Python value types inside a response payload. Operation and dispatch Selects a handler and template when one URL has several operations.

The template describes the JSON envelope. It does not validate the payload's runtime type. Use type annotations and the payload definitions in bumper/web/payloads.py to make the payload shape clear to mypy and tests.

docs.title: 🛣️ Register a route
docs.text:
Every plugin module owns a web.RouteTableDef named routes. The package defines its prefix once in its __init__.py; modules use that prefix when registering paths. The web plugin loader discovers plugin modules, so a new module under bumper/web/plugins/ does not need a second route-registration edit.

from aiohttp import web
from aiohttp.web_request import Request

from bumper.web.envelope import GL_V1, bind

from . import BASE_URL

routes = web.RouteTableDef()


@routes.view(f"{BASE_URL}user/getBackupEmailByAccount")
@bind(GL_V1)
async def _handle_get_backup_email_by_account(request: Request) -> dict[str, str | None]:
    """Return the backup email fields expected by this endpoint."""
    return {"backUpEmail": None, "displayEmail": None}

Decorators are applied from the bottom up: bind wraps the handler first, then routes.view registers the wrapped handler. routes.view accepts any HTTP method. Prefer routes.get, routes.post, and the other method-specific registrations when the endpoint has a fixed method. Paths are case-sensitive.

A bound handler returns only the payload. It does not add code, ret, message, data, or other envelope fields itself. The binder owns those fields, including the error response shape.

docs.title: 📦 What @bind does
docs.text:
bind is implemented in bumper/web/envelope/binder.py:

  1. It calls the handler with the Request.
  2. If the handler returns a StreamResponse such as web.Response, it passes that response through unchanged. This is for files, images, and other raw documents.
  3. Otherwise, it passes the returned payload to Template.render and returns the rendered JSON.
  4. An ApiError is rendered using the template's ErrorShape, not its success shape. An uncaught exception is logged and returned with that error shape and HTTP status 500. web.HTTPException is re-raised.

For example, a handler bound to GL_V1 can return {"items": []}. The client receives the payload inside data, plus the GL_V1 success fields. If the handler raises ApiError(msg="No account", code=ERR_TOKEN_INVALID), the same route returns the GL_V1 error envelope. The handler does not need to choose either envelope itself.

Returning web.json_response(...) from a bound handler is usually wrong: it bypasses the template and its error handling. Return a payload instead. Return a Response only when the endpoint really is a raw response.

docs.title: 🧱 Template fields
docs.text:
Template is defined in bumper/web/envelope/templates.py. Its settings control the outer shape:

Setting Effect code, code_key Adds a status value under a key such as code. Use code=None when there is no status field or the key carries payload data. data_key Places the handler's payload under this key. None makes the payload flat. data_optional Omits the payload key when the handler returns None. Otherwise, None is serialized as JSON null. flat Merges a mapping payload into the response body instead of nesting it. result Adds a fixed result pair such as ("ret", "ok"). msg Adds a fixed message pair such as ("message", "success"). success Adds the boolean success field when set. time, time_value Adds the current time in milliseconds, or a fixed time value. todo Adds "todo": "result". extra Adds fixed side-car fields alongside the payload. error Selects the separate error envelope for the template.

ErrorShape controls failure keys such as errno, error, ret, todo, success, and time. A success template and its error shape need not have the same keys. Check both before using a template.

docs.title: 🧾 Choose the response shape
docs.text:
Start from the response contract of the endpoint or operation being added. Choose the template by the JSON shape, not by which template name seems cleanest.

Client-visible response Use Common location code: "0000", msg, data, success, and millisecond time GL_V1 Modern private API routes and global auth routes. code: 0, message, ret: "ok", and data LEGACY Standard /api/... JSON endpoints. Legacy envelope without a success ret field LEGACY_NO_RET or another matching LEGACY variant Endpoints whose success response omits ret. Legacy envelope with a flat payload and todo: "result" LEGACY_FLAT /api/users/user.do operations. Legacy envelope with todo: "result", ret: "ok", and data TODO_RET Older dispatcher endpoints such as app.do. {"todo":"result","result":"ok","code":...} where code is payload AUTH The newauth.do auth-code exchange. {"ret":"ok"} with no payload RET_ONLY Operations that answer only with a result flag. A file, image, or document body No template, or a bound handler returning Response Photo downloads and document endpoints. HTTP 200, empty body, outcome in x-ngiot-* headers response_ngiot_* helpers /api/iot/endpoint/control. This is not a JSON envelope.

LEGACY_BARE, LEGACY_MSG, and LEGACY_SUCCESS cover other legacy variants. Read their definitions and error shapes in templates.py rather than deriving one from a similar-looking template.

docs.title: Typed payloads
docs.text:
The payload type is separate from the envelope template. Define or reuse a TypedDict in bumper/web/payloads.py when a payload has named fields:

from typing import TypedDict


class ExampleInfo(TypedDict):
    """The information returned by the example endpoint."""

    id: str
    enabled: bool


@routes.get(f"{PREFIX}/example/info")
@bind(LEGACY)
async def _handle_example_info(_: Request) -> ExampleInfo:
    """Return the example payload, not the legacy envelope."""
    return {"id": "example", "enabled": True}

Use NotRequired[...] for keys that are genuinely optional in the payload. Do not make a field optional just because a value is unavailable in one test; the response shape is part of the client contract. Template.render accepts Any and does not enforce TypedDict at runtime, so keep the annotations, builder, and tests aligned.

docs.title: 🔀 One path, several operations
docs.text:
Some endpoints select their behavior by todo or td in the request body. Each operation can have a different response shape, so define an Operation table and dispatch through it. Do not bind one envelope around the whole path.

from collections.abc import Mapping
from typing import Any

from aiohttp import web
from aiohttp.web_request import Request
from bumper.web.envelope import LEGACY_FLAT
from bumper.web.operations import Operation, dispatch

from . import PREFIX

routes = web.RouteTableDef()
USER_DO_OPERATIONS: dict[str, Operation] = {}
routes.post(f"{PREFIX}/users/user.do")(dispatch(USER_DO_OPERATIONS, LEGACY_FLAT))


async def _handle_get_device_list(request: Request, post_body: Mapping[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Return the payload for this user.do operation."""
    return {"devices": []}


USER_DO_OPERATIONS.update(
    {"GetDeviceList": Operation(LEGACY_FLAT, _handle_get_device_list)},
)

The dispatcher reads the configured discriminator, invokes the operation handler, and renders its payload with that operation's template. The dispatcher template is the failure shape for an unknown operation. Operation handlers return payloads, not envelopes.

docs.title: ⚡ Quick checklist
docs.text:
Before implementing a route, answer these questions:

  1. Is it a JSON envelope, a raw file/document response, or the NGIoT header protocol?
  2. What exact success keys and value types does the client expect?
  3. What exact failure shape does this endpoint use? Can the handler raise ApiError and let the binder shape it?
  4. Does one path have multiple todo/td operations? If so, choose a template per operation with dispatch.
  5. Does the payload have a reusable typed shape? Put that TypedDict or its builder in bumper/web/payloads.py.
  6. Does the route path use the package prefix and the observed path casing?

If the answer shape is not known, do not invent a new template. Find an existing matching operation or gather the missing response contract first.

docs.title: 🧪 Keep the response contract checked
docs.text:
• Put each route in the plugin module that owns the API path. Keep the route declaration near the handler or operation table.
  • Add handler and payload tests under tests/web/, mirroring the source path.
  • scripts/api/api-table.py shows each route's bound response shape.
  • tests/web/routes.txt and tests/web/shapes.txt pin route registration and template selection. The pre-commit hook updates them when web routes change.
  • tests/web/response_shapes.json and tests/web/response_shapes_bumper.json check response keys and Python value types. A new key or changed type needs a reason in the response contract.
  • Run uv run --active --frozen pytest tests/web, the linters, and uv run --active --frozen mkdocs build --strict before contributing.

The core definitions are in bumper/web/envelope/templates.py, bumper/web/envelope/binder.py, and bumper/web/operations.py.

docs.title: Certificates for Bumper
docs.text: Bumper requires TLS certificates to communicate securely with Ecovacs devices and apps.

docs.title: 🔄 Automatic Generation
docs.text:
Bumper generates certificates as part of its normal startup if the required files are missing. This happens automatically; no manual generation command is needed. The Python startup and helper script use the same certificate filenames in the certs/ directory relative to their working directory.

You can also create the files ahead of startup with the helper:

bash scripts/certs/create-cert.sh

For the checked-in Compose and Swarm files, there is an additional constraint: they load the certificate files as host-backed Docker configs before starting the Bumper container. Those host files must exist before deployment, so create them with the helper above when using these files. Bumper's automatic generation still applies to startup modes where it can write to its certificate directory.

For a robot that requires RSA keys, set CERT_KEY_TYPE=rsa when Bumper generates a new certificate set. Bumper keeps an existing certificate set; changing CERT_KEY_TYPE does not convert certificates that were already generated.

docs.title: 📂 Generated Files
docs.text:
When certificate generation runs, Bumper creates the following files in certs/:

File Description ca.key Root CA private key ca.crt Root CA certificate bumper.key Server private key bumper.crt Server certificate ca.pem Server key, server certificate and CA certificate in one file

Bumper skips generation if all certificate files already exist.

ca.pem contains the server private key. Treat it as a secret and do not share it; it is only meant for a local proxy such as mitmproxy.

docs.title: 🔧 Custom Certificates
docs.text:
If you prefer to use your own certificates, place them in the certs/ directory before starting Bumper:

  • ca.crt, bumper.key, bumper.crt for Bumper
  • ca.pem for mitmproxy (optional)

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Configure certificate paths via environment variables (defaults shown):

BUMPER_CERTS=$PWD/certs

Or point directly to full paths:

BUMPER_CA_CERT=certs/ca.crt
BUMPER_CA_KEY=certs/ca.key
BUMPER_CA_PEM=certs/ca.pem
BUMPER_CERT=certs/bumper.crt
BUMPER_KEY=certs/bumper.key

docs.title: mitmproxy
docs.text:
Mount ca.pem into your mitmproxy container or CLI:

docker run --rm -it \
  -v $PWD/certs/ca.pem:/home/mitm/ca.pem:ro \
  mitmproxy/mitmproxy mitmweb \
    --certs '*=/home/mitm/ca.pem'

Note: ca.pem is only needed by mitmproxy; Bumper uses individual CRT/KEY files.

docs.title: DNS Configuration for Bumper
docs.text: To intercept and redirect traffic from Ecovacs robots and the official app to your local Bumper server, configure your network’s DNS resolver to override specific Ecovacs domains to your server’s IP.

docs.title: 🔧 Recommended: OPNsense + Unbound DNS
docs.text:
If you're using OPNsense as your router/firewall, Unbound DNS is the default resolver. Override domain resolution by adding host overrides:

  1. Login to the OPNsense web interface.
  2. Navigate to Services → Unbound DNS → Overrides.
  3. Under Host Overrides, click Add and set:
    • Host: *
    • Domain: ecouser.net
    • IP: <BUMPER_SERVER_IP> (e.g. 192.168.1.100)
  4. Repeat for each domain pattern:
    • *.ecouser.com
    • *.ecovacs.com
    • *.ecouser.net
    • *.ecovacs.net
  5. Click Apply to reload Unbound.

These wildcard entries catch all subdomains under the specified domain.

docs.title: 📦 Alternative: dnsmasq / Pi-hole
docs.text:
If you're using DNSMasq directly or via Pi-hole, create a custom config file:

/etc/dnsmasq.d/02-bumper.conf

address=/ecouser.com/<BUMPER_SERVER_IP>
address=/ecouser.net/<BUMPER_SERVER_IP>
address=/ecovacs.com/<BUMPER_SERVER_IP>
address=/ecovacs.net/<BUMPER_SERVER_IP>

Replace <BUMPER_SERVER_IP> with your server’s local IP (e.g. 192.168.1.100).

Apply changes:

  • dnsmasq: sudo systemctl reload dnsmasq
  • Pi-hole: pihole restartdns or via the web UI

docs.title: ⚠️ Pi-hole v6 and dnsmasq.d
docs.text:
Pi-hole v6 does not ingest custom configs in /etc/dnsmasq.d/ by default; this behavior is disabled in FTL. discourse.pi-hole You must explicitly re-enable it:

  • ENV: add as environment variable:
    • FTLCONF_misc.dnsmasq_d=true
  • Via GUI: in the Pi-hole web UI, go to Settings > All settings page - Miscellaneous and enable the option.

Without this, custom 02-bumper.conf-style entries will be silently ignored, explaining why DNS redirects may appear not to work.

docs.title: 📋 Notes on Domain Patterns
docs.text:
If overriding DNS for top-level domains (like *.ecovacs.com) isn’t supported in your DNS setup, you’ll need to manually configure each relevant subdomain used by the app or robot to point to your Bumper server.

EcoVacs robots and the companion app connect to a variety of domains depending on the country or region selected during setup. The Bumper project doesn’t care which exact domain is used-as long as the request is forwarded, it will be intercepted correctly.

🧠 The app dynamically retrieves its domain list from the endpoint: https://{region}.ecouser.net/api/appsvr/service/list This means the required domains may vary across models, regions, and firmware versions.

docs.title: Replacement Examples
docs.text:
Most domains follow patterns based on country or region codes:

  • {countrycode}
    • If you see eco-{countrycode}-api.ecovacs.com and you're in the US/North America, use: eco-us-api.ecovacs.com
    • Note: {countrycode} may also be region codes like EU, WW, or CN.
  • {region}
    • If you see portal-{region}.ecouser.net and you're in North America, use: portal-na.ecouser.net
    • Note: {region} values may also include eu, cn, or ww.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• ✅ If your DNS supports wildcard or full-domain overrides, use them to catch all subdomains at once.
  • ❌ If it does not, you must manually define each used domain/subdomain to ensure proper redirection.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
⚠️ Disclaimer: This document is a work in progress and may contain inaccuracies or incomplete sections. Some parts serve as placeholders and require further refinement. Please refer to the source code for authoritative information, and feel free to submit corrections or improvements.

Bumper recreates Ecovacs’s central cloud services locally, so your robots and app work seamlessly within your network. It supports both XMPP and MQTT protocols.

docs.title: 🧩 Services
docs.text: Service Description Ports Module Path Web Server Handles discovery, login, REST API for commands and status 443, 8007 bumper.web.server XMPP Server Relays XML stanzas between client and robot over XMPP 5223 bumper.xmpp.xmpp MQTT Broker Manages MQTT topics for telemetry and commands 1883, 8883 bumper.mqtt.server

docs.title: 🔒 App / Authentication
docs.text:
Bumper recreates the account and token plumbing the app expects, but it does not verify Ecovacs request signatures. The app logs in with an account name, receives an opaque access token, exchanges an IoT token for an auth code, and then receives OAuth tokens. The same auth code links the account to the XMPP or MQTT transport.

The account key is separate from the TLS key. The private half stays in the data directory, so Bumper can read the fields the app encrypts and no other server can.

One account has three public ids: A for the account, U for the unified identity, and I for the IoT session. Each app installation has a client id and resource (K/R), with its own token row. A BumperUser owns its app devices, while every local account receives the shared robot inventory; legacy ids are aliases on that same record. This keeps parallel app clients separate without creating duplicate accounts.

See Authentication for the full flow, the trust model, and the known gaps.

docs.title: 🔒 Login / Authentication / REST API
docs.text:
Bumper’s Web Server module simulates the Ecovacs REST API for login and command routing:

  • Discovery: Robots and the mobile app retrieve service endpoints (XMPP broker or MQTT server addresses) via HTTPS requests to the discovery URL exposed on ports 443/8007.
  • Authentication: The app submits account data; a normal login creates or finds the local account and returns an access token, while a session check resolves the existing account by the app device. Later calls name the account with that token or with a user id. The HTTP layer does not verify request signatures.
  • Command Routing: When the app issues a command (for example, start cleaning), it makes a REST call against Bumper’s web service. The request is enqueued and handed off to the MQTT helper or forwarded to the XMPP server, depending on the robot’s protocol.
  • Status Queries: The app can poll for the robot’s latest state via REST endpoints, which query the latest telemetry stored by Bumper.

These paths mirror the patterns the app expects, so the app works unmodified.

docs.title: 🔗 XMPP Protocol
docs.text:
Example Models: Ozmo 601, Ozmo 930

  1. Discovery
    • Robot and app request XMPP server info from /discover.
    • Bumper returns its own hostname/IP for XMPP.
  2. Connection
    • Both robot and app open TLS on port 5223 to Bumper’s XMPP Server.
  3. Message Relay
    • Bumper maintains separate sessions for each side and forwards XML stanzas.
    • Commands (e.g., start/stop) and status (e.g., battery) are exchanged as XMPP messages.
  4. Keep‑Alive
    • Bumper responds to XMPP pings and sends heartbeats to prevent timeouts.

Tip: The Ecovacs app attempts XMPP first; if no valid messages, it falls back to MQTT models.

docs.title: ☁️ MQTT Protocol
docs.text:
Example Models: Deebot 600, 900, 901, Ozmo 950

  1. Broker Connection
    • Robot connects to Bumper’s MQTT Broker on 8883 (TLS) or 1883 (plain).
    • Subscribes to p2p/<device_id> for incoming commands.
  2. Telemetry Publishing
    • Robot publishes JSON status (battery, location) to attr/<device_id> at intervals.
  3. Command Delivery
    • App issues POST /api/command to Web Server.
    • Web Server forwards the command to the Helper Bot.
    • Helper Bot publishes the command to p2p/<device_id>.
  4. Response Handling
    • Robot executes the command and publishes results back to p2p/<device_id> or rsp/<device_id>.
    • Helper Bot stores responses and makes them available via REST for the app.

docs.title: ⚙️ Helper Bot
docs.text:
• An internal MQTT client that bridges REST API calls to MQTT topics.
  • Connects with a fixed client id that the broker accepts before any other check.
  • Correlates request/response pairs by message ID for REST replies.

For further details, see the source modules in bumper/web/server.py, bumper/xmpp/xmpp.py, and bumper/mqtt/server.py.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Bumper reproduces the account and token plumbing the Ecovacs app expects, but it does not reproduce the cloud's security model. The app must work on a LAN without an Ecovacs account, so Bumper accepts the identity the client names and issues its own tokens. This page describes both sides: what the official app does, and what Bumper does with it.

The important consequence is at the top: HTTP request signatures are not verified. JWTs are verified when Bumper uses their claims as proof of account ownership.

docs.title: 🔐 Trust model
docs.text:
Bumper is built for a trusted local network. It:

  • accepts an account name without checking a password,
  • issues an app token for any account name,
  • accepts the app's encrypted fields but does not verify who sent them,
  • decodes some bearer-token claims for request context without checking the signature,
  • lets the MQTT and XMPP servers skip token checks because USE_AUTH is False.

The TLS CA is the real trust boundary. A device that trusts Bumper's CA can talk to Bumper; Bumper does not establish a second identity for it. Do not expose the web, MQTT, or XMPP listeners to an untrusted network.

USE_AUTH in bumper/utils/settings.py is a code constant, not an environment variable. Setting it to True enables secret checks in MQTT and XMPP. The checks accept a live portal token, auth code, or IT token, or a valid access JWT signed by this Bumper instance. It does not make the HTTP API verify request signatures.

docs.title: 🧩 Identity layers
docs.text:
The account and each app installation have separate identities:

Identity Used by Shape / role Account id (A) app and modern API YYYYMMDDHHMMSS_<32 lowercase hex> Unified id (U) IoT auth-code exchange same shape as A, generated independently IoT id (I) OAuth and legacy transports 16 lowercase letters or digits Client id (K) OAuth and app-installation row 24 lowercase hex characters Resource (R) XMPP/MQTT connection and client client-provided resource string App device id (D) app path and device ownership generated by the app Robot id robot, MQTT, XMPP serial number or device id, depending on robot generation

Bumper stores the account in BumperUser (bumper/web/utils/models.py) and the short-lived session data in Token (bumper/db/tokens.py). The user record carries A, U, I, the login name, aliases, app device ids, and the robots known to the local service. Each local account receives the shared robot list. Each token row carries one portal token and its related IT token, auth code, K, R, and device id. ClientRepo stores the live connection state for each app client/resource.

docs.title: How the user id is made
docs.text:
New accounts receive independent A, U, and I values. A is also the internal userid of a newly created account. Existing records keep their internal id; when first used, Bumper adopts a presented public id into an empty field or generates a missing id, and retains the old id as an alias. The pre-redesign 20-character SHA-256-derived id is recognized as a legacy alias, not generated as the new public account id.

Login resolves the provided name case-insensitively. For login2, Bumper decrypts encryptAccount with its local account key and stores the result as the login name. The encrypted password is accepted but not checked. If no name is provided, the configured USER_USERNAME_DEFAULT is used.

docs.title: One account, several names
docs.text:
The app does not use one name for an account. It logs in with a login name, uses A and U during the modern flow, and uses I for OAuth and legacy transports. Each app installation also has a device id and client/resource pair. Bumper keeps one BumperUser per account and resolves its public ids and legacy ids as aliases (bumper/db/identity.py). Accounts with different login names remain separate unless a shared device, presented account id, or valid token links them.

When a name resolves to a second user record and the link is proven - the token names one record and the request names the other, or the app device is bound to one record and the request names the other - the older record wins. The duplicate's devices, robots, homes, tokens, and clients move to the older record, and its id becomes an alias. Startup also merges duplicate public ids, login names, and app-device ownership before reconciling client rows. Rows with no account owner are removed; rows carrying an account alias are moved to the canonical account. Distinct client ids or resources remain distinct rows.

checkLogin never creates a user. It resolves an unknown name by the app device and fails if neither is known, because a check is not a registration. The normal login creates an account when the login name is new, then binds the device to it. Reusing the same login name resolves to the same account.

docs.title: 🌐 The official flow
docs.text:
The current app uses two API families at once. The account screens and the login handshake use the modern *.ecovacs.com API. The robot-facing calls and the OAuth exchange use the legacy *.ecouser.net API.

docs.title: 1. The app reads the account key
docs.text:
The app asks the modern API for configuration:

GET /v1/private/{country}/{language}/{deviceId}/{appType}/{version}/{deviceType}/{aid}/common/getConfig?keys=PUBLIC.KEY.CONFIG

The answer contains the RSA public key as base64 DER. The app uses it to encrypt fields such as encryptAccount, encryptPwd, encryptEmail, and the backup address before they leave the phone. The private key never leaves the server.

Bumper serves the public half at the same path. The key is generated once and stored in BUMPER_ACCOUNT_KEY (default ${BUMPER_DATA}/account.key) with mode 0600. It is separate from the TLS server key on purpose: the app needs RSA, the default TLS key is EC, and rotating the TLS certificate must not rotate the account key.

docs.title: 2. The app logs in
docs.text:
The modern login path is:

GET /v2/private/{country}/{language}/{deviceId}/{appType}/{version}/{deviceType}/{aid}/user/login2

The request carries encryptAccount and encryptPwd, plus the signing query parameters described below. Bumper decrypts the account name, resolves or creates one account, binds the app device id, and issues a portal token. The answer contains accessToken, uid (A), ucUid (U), loginName, username, country, and the response fields expected by the app.

If the account is new, the cloud may answer with loginResult: HIGH_RISK and loginRiskScene: NEW_DEVICE, and the app asks for an email code before it continues. Bumper answers success directly.

docs.title: 3. The app exchanges the account token for an IoT token
docs.text:
The app calls the OpenAPI host:

GET /v1/global/auth/getAuthCode?uid={uid}&accessToken={token}&bizType=ECOVACS_IOT&deviceId={deviceId}

The answer is an IT token:

{
    "code": "0000",
    "data": {
        "authCode": "GLOBAL_APP_ECOVACS_IOT_<32 hex>",
        "ecovacsUid": "<user id>"
    }
}

Despite the field name, this authCode is the IT token. It is attached to the token row identified by the presented access token. The app then posts it to the legacy login:

POST /newauth.do
{"todo": "OLoginByITToken", "itToken": "GLOBAL_APP_ECOVACS_IOT_<32 hex>"}

The answer is the real auth code:

{ "todo": "result", "result": "ok", "authCode": "<32 hex>" }

docs.title: 4. The app gets OAuth tokens
docs.text:
The auth code is exchanged on the legacy API:

GET /api/appsvr/oauth_callback?state={"cid":"<client id>"}&code={authCode}

The answer carries userId (I), access_token, refresh_token, and expire_at in milliseconds. The access token is a JWT. Its claims name the client (c = K), the user (u = I), the client resource (r = R), and the auth code (ac).

The app refreshes the pair through:

GET /api/appsvr/oauth/token?grant_type=refresh_token&refresh_token={jwt}&client_id={client id}

The refresh token is the same kind of JWT with t: "r"; the access token has t: "a".

docs.title: 5. Later calls
docs.text:
The modern API sends the access token as accessToken in the query string and also as authorization: Bearer <jwt> on some calls. The legacy API sends the opaque token as token or accessToken, depending on the endpoint.

The MQTT and XMPP transports resolve the presented IoT name and secret to the canonical account. With USE_AUTH=True, an access JWT must be signed by this Bumper instance. Connection rows retain their client/resource identity, so parallel app installations do not overwrite one another.

docs.title: ✍️ Signing on the modern API
docs.text:
The modern API adds five query parameters to every call:

Parameter Meaning authAppkey The app key. The app ships several, for the app and for OpenAPI. authTimespan The app clock in milliseconds, plus the server offset. authTimeZone The device timezone, for example GMT+2. requestId A per-request random id. authSign A digest over the app key, the sorted parameters, and a native secret.

The reference implementation builds the canonical string from the app key and the sorted query parameters, appends the secret, and digests the result. The keys and secrets are resolved from the native libeco-network.so library, not from Java constants.

Bumper ignores all five parameters. It does not reject a missing, stale, or wrong authSign. This is intentional for a LAN server: the app must work with a clock that is not synchronized to Ecovacs, and the signature protects a cloud account Bumper does not have.

The legacy API has a parallel scheme. com.ecovacs.lib_iot_client sends appid, ts, and sign, where sign is SHA1(appid + APP_SECRET + ts). Bumper does not verify those either. The app ships several app ids and secrets for the ecovacs and yeedi brands; Bumper does not need them.

docs.title: Login and tokens
docs.text:
bumper/web/auth_service.py:login serves both user/login and user/checkLogin on v1 and v2. The behavior is:

  1. Decrypt encryptAccount when present, then resolve the login name.
  2. Create an account with A, U, and I when the login name is new.
  3. Bind the app device id to that account.
  4. Remove expired token rows for the account.
  5. Generate a fresh opaque portal token and store a row for this login.
  6. Return uid=A and ucUid=U in the login document.

checkLogin never creates a user. An unknown name is resolved by the app device, and a request that matches neither is rejected. A check with a valid accessToken returns the same token. A check without a token issues a new one for the known account; an invalid supplied token is rejected. The portal token is opaque; it is not a JWT.

The portal-token lifetime is TOKEN_VALIDITY_SECONDS (30 days). Expiry removes the token row, including its IT token and auth code. A check with an expired portal token fails rather than silently replacing it. The modern /v1/global/auth/getAuthCode path requires a live portal token.

docs.title: GetAuthCode
docs.text:
There are two paths:

  • /v1/global/auth/getAuthCode and the private getAuthCode endpoint return the IT token in authCode. A live access token is required, and the IT token is attached to the token row that access token identifies.
  • api/users/user.do with todo: GetAuthCode returns the legacy auth code in code. It uses the token row named by the request when possible, or creates a portal-token row when no row is available.

Both paths resolve the presented account names to one user. A JWT claim is used to link accounts only after verify_jwt checks the signature, expiry, and access-token type. The IT token and auth code remain attached to the same client token row, so the next exchanges preserve the client boundary.

docs.title: newauth.do
docs.text:
bumper/web/single_paths.py:handle_new_auth accepts only todo: OLoginByITToken. It calls get_new_auth, which looks up the IT token, rejects an expired row, and returns the existing or newly generated auth code. The request's clientID and resource are stored on that same token and client row. The response is bound to the AUTH shape, so the answer is {"todo": "result", "result": "ok", "authCode": "..."}.

loginByItToken on api/users/user.do answers with userId=I, the portal token from the matching client row, and last, its remaining lifetime in milliseconds. The IT token is only the input of the exchange.

docs.title: OAuth and JWT
docs.text:
oauth_callback resolves the auth code to its token row, reads that row's client id and resource, and generates two JWTs with generate_jwt_helper:

  • access token: t: "a", expiry ACCESS_TOKEN_VALIDITY_SECONDS (30 minutes)
  • refresh token: t: "r", expiry REFRESH_TOKEN_VALIDITY_SECONDS (30 days)

The token row remains until the refresh token expires. A successful OAuth exchange moves its expiry to the refresh token's expiry, and each successful refresh extends the session. This lets the app resume after an idle period without keeping the access JWT long-lived. Logout removes the row and revokes the refresh session.

The tokens are signed with the TLS server key (bumper_isc.server_key) and the algorithm in TOKEN_JWT_ALG. The default follows the certificate key type: ES256 for EC and RS256 for RSA.

bumper/web/jwt.py has two readers. get_jwt_details and extract_jwt_details decode the claims without checking the signature for the request context. verify_jwt loads the public key from the TLS certificate, checks the signature, the expiry, and the token type, and is the only reader that may be used as proof. The legacy GetAuthCode call, the refresh grant, and transport authentication use verify_jwt; a refresh token is not accepted where an access token is required. Account resolution also uses a JWT only after this check, even when USE_AUTH is off, because the claim can move a name between accounts.

docs.title: The account key
docs.text:
bumper/utils/account_key.py owns the RSA key used for encrypted account fields:

  • account_public_key() returns base64 DER, which is what PUBLIC.KEY.CONFIG serves.
  • decrypt_account_field() decodes base64, decrypts with PKCS#1 v1.5, and returns the stripped UTF-8 text, or None on a malformed or foreign value.
  • _load_or_create() generates a 2048-bit RSA key on first use, writes it with O_EXCL at mode 0600, and re-reads it if another process won the race.

The private key is not used to sign JWTs or TLS certificates. It only decrypts the fields the app encrypts with the public key.

If the key changes, the app keeps the old public key for the life of its process. Force-stop the app after replacing account.key; otherwise the next email or password change returns 1008 because the ciphertext cannot be decrypted.

docs.title: Email, password, and OTP
docs.text:
Endpoint Behavior user/sendEmailVerifyCode Returns a fresh verifyId UUID. No mail is sent. user/checkEmailVerifyByScene Accepts EMAIL_VERIFY_CODE (default 666666). user/bindEmail2 Checks verifyCode, decrypts encryptEmail, stores it as email. user/addBackupEmail Decrypts encryptEmail and stores it as backup_email. user/modifyPassword Returns success with data: null. The password is not stored. device/otp/generate Returns a six digit code and stores it for DEVICE_OTP_TTL_SECONDS. device/verify/check Accepts the code while it is in the TTL.

bindEmail2 and addBackupEmail use claimed_userid, which reads userid, uid, a userid header, or the auth query object. None of those is signed. The address is stored only, not verified against a mailbox.

The OTP flow is equally local: the code is generated, returned to the caller, and accepted for the TTL. It is not a security control against a LAN peer.

docs.title: Robot transports
docs.text:
The app reaches the robot through XMPP or MQTT, depending on the model.

XMPP (bumper/xmpp/xmpp.py)

  • The app and the robot connect over TLS on port 5223.
  • SASL PLAIN carries an authzid, the user id, and a password. The password is either a bare secret or 0/<resource>/<secret>. Bumper reads the user id and the resource from the NUL-separated payload and joins the rest of the password after the resource, because a JWT never contains /.
  • A client with a devclass is a robot: Bumper stores it as a bot and accepts it without a token check.
  • A client without a devclass is the app. Bumper resolves the name through the portal token, the auth code, the IT token, or a signed access JWT to the canonical account and records the client under that account and resource. With USE_AUTH=True the secret must verify with identity.verify_transport_secret; with USE_AUTH=False the client is accepted and a name is adopted only when it already resolves or a valid secret links it.
  • The bound JID is <uid>@<devclass>.ecorobot.net/atom for a robot and <uid>@<server>/<resource> for the app.

MQTT (bumper/mqtt/server.py)

  • The broker listens on 1883 (plain) and 8883 (TLS).
  • A client id has the form <did>@<class id>/<resource>.
  • The class id decides the side: USER_CLASS_IDS (ecouser, bumper, USER) means app, anything else means robot.
  • The username may carry base64 app headers after a backtick; Bumper decodes them for logging and keeps the first segment as the username.
  • The helper bot uses a fixed client id and is accepted before any other check.
  • Bumper resolves the presented client name to the canonical account before it stores the client. Each client id/resource has its own row, so one account can keep parallel app installations and transport connections.
  • With USE_AUTH=False, Bumper accepts the password as-is. With USE_AUTH=True, the password must be a portal token, an auth code, an IT token, or a signed access JWT issued for that account.
  • A password file can also hold username:hash entries for broker users. It is read from ${BUMPER_DATA}/passwd.

The helper bot is Bumper's own client. It connects to the broker with the fixed HELPER_BOT_CLIENT_ID, bypasses authentication, and is the only component that writes the firmware version it learns from a robot into the database.

docs.title: 📱 The app on the wire
docs.text:
These facts come from the app package and are useful when a login fails:

  • The legacy client is com.ecovacs.lib_iot_client; it builds appid, ts, and sign in NetRequestUtil.
  • The modern client is com.eco.econetwork; SigningInterceptor and OpenSigningInterceptor add authAppkey, authTimespan, authTimeZone, requestId, and authSign.
  • The app reads PUBLIC.KEY.CONFIG before it encrypts account fields.
  • The app pins no certificate except the MQTT broker. The MQTT pin is embedded in a classes*.dex; scripts/app/apk-patch/patch-mqtt-trust.py removes it so Paho falls back to the platform store.
  • The NGIoT channel uses a native mbedTLS stack. It reads the system CA store and ignores the user store, so a user-installed Bumper CA does not cover it. If only that channel fails, suspect this before the certificate names.
  • The app's account screens need React Native and Hermes. A white screen there is usually a missing libhermes.so for the emulator ABI, not a Bumper auth failure.

The app package is the source for these details.

docs.title: 🤖 The robot on the wire
docs.text:
The robot does not log in with an Ecovacs account. It is provisioned with the server address and a local identity, and then it connects:

  • Older robots use XMPP with the serial number as the user id and atom as the resource.
  • Newer robots use MQTT with the serial number or device id as the client id, the model as the class id, and a resource name.
  • The auth code is the link from the account login to the transport. The robot receives it through the app's provisioning step, not through the cloud login.
  • TLS is verified against the CA the robot trusts. That CA is the one Bumper serves at /ca-certificates.tar.gz.

When Bumper sees a robot for the first time, the MQTT or XMPP login creates the bot record. Later calls use that record to resolve the serial number, model, and resource.

docs.title: 🗺️ Code map
docs.text: Concern File Login, tokens, auth codes bumper/web/auth_service.py JWT decoding and checking bumper/web/jwt.py Request identity helpers bumper/web/context.py Account names and aliases bumper/db/identity.py Public account id shapes bumper/utils/account_ids.py Token and user records bumper/db/tokens.py, bumper/db/users.py Client records bumper/db/clients.py Account RSA key bumper/utils/account_key.py Auth endpoints (v1) bumper/web/plugins/v1/private/user.py Auth endpoints (v2) bumper/web/plugins/v2/private/user.py OpenAPI auth code bumper/web/plugins/v1/global_auth.py newauth.do bumper/web/single_paths.py OAuth callback bumper/web/plugins/api/appsvr.py XMPP authentication bumper/xmpp/xmpp.py MQTT authentication bumper/mqtt/server.py OTP endpoints bumper/web/plugins/v1/private/device.py

docs.title: ⚠️ Known gaps
docs.text:
• authSign is not verified. A wrong signature is accepted.
  • appid, ts, and the legacy sign are not verified.
  • The account password is ignored. Any password logs in.
  • Some request-context helpers decode JWT claims without checking the signature. Account linking and transport authentication use verify_jwt, which checks the signature, expiry, and token type.
  • USE_AUTH is a code constant, not an environment setting.
  • The auth code and IT token are removed when their portal/refresh session row expires. The legacy GetAuthCode path can create a fresh row; modern getAuthCode requires a live portal token and the client must log in again.
  • A logout with a recognized token revokes only its client row. A logout with no token revokes every token and client for the account; an unknown supplied token does not log out unrelated clients.
  • The email verification code is fixed. Bumper never sends mail.
  • The OTP is returned to the caller and accepted for its TTL. It is a UX emulation, not a second factor.

These are deliberate for a self-hosted LAN replacement. Treat the network and the CA as the security boundary, not the application tokens.

docs.title: Defeating Certificate Pinning in the Ecovacs Home App
docs.text:
This guide covers how to make the Ecovacs Home Android app trust your own Bumper instance, so the app talks only to your LAN.

⚠️ Disclaimer:

Modifying the Ecovacs app may break future updates. Proceed at your own risk.

docs.title: 📋 Methods
docs.text:
Five ways to do this are documented below. Each needs different tools, so check its own Needs: line. Only the first is maintained.

Method Needs MQTT works Maintained Automated script docker yes yes Automated script (legacy) docker - no Manual apk-mitm node, npm, java, adb - no Manual apktool java, adb - no Manual android-unpinner python, java, adb - no

The three manual methods are reference material: they work in principle but are untested against current app versions. None of them applies the MQTT patch, so with those the web API works and robot control depends on app version.

docs.title: 🚀 Automated script (latest)
docs.text: Needs: docker, and nothing else. The download, the patching and the signing all run inside a container, so your host stays clean. You also need adb and certs/ca.crt (see Create Certificates) for the device steps below, plus an arm64 device - see Device requirement.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
1. Downloads the app (XAPK or APK) and unpacks its splits.
  2. Sets android:debuggable="true" in the manifest, which activates the app's own <debug-overrides><certificates src="user"/>. That is what makes the platform trust your user-installed CA.
  3. Makes the certificate Ecovacs hardcodes for MQTT unusable, so that channel also falls back to the platform trust store.
  4. Runs zipalign and re-signs every split with a key kept in certs/.
  5. Verifies the result and prints the adb command to install it.

Steps 2 and 3 are both required. Without step 3 no robot command arrives, because every command is relayed over MQTT.

scripts/app/create-unpinned-app.sh writes the installable APKs to data/<app-name>/.

scripts/app/create-unpinned-app.sh

All of it runs in a container (bumper-apk-tool: JDK, Android build-tools, python3, curl). The only things written outside the container are data/<app-name>/ and the signing key certs/bumper-apk.jks; the download, the unpacked splits and the intermediate copies all disappear with the container. Editing a patcher only rebuilds the image's last layer.

1. Install the APKs. The script prints the exact command:

adb install-multiple --no-incremental data/<app-name>/*.apk

2. Install Bumper's CA on the phone as a user CA certificate: Settings → Security → Encryption & credentials → Install a certificate → CA certificate, and select certs/ca.crt. The script does not do this for you.

3. Point the app at your Bumper instance (see DNS Setup).

docs.title: Device requirement
docs.text:
An arm64 Android device, or an arm64 emulator. The account screens are React Native, so they need libhermes.so. base.apk contains no native code at all - every .so lives in the per-ABI split - and SoLoader searches only lib/<SUPPORTED_ABIS[0]> inside the APKs, one ABI, not a loop.

An x86_64 emulator reports SUPPORTED_ABIS: x86_64, arm64-v8a, and the app publishes no x86_64 build at any version, so libhermes.so is never found and the main activity dies in onCreate with SoLoaderDSONotFoundError. That is the white screen. Downgrading the app does not help: React Native and Hermes are already present in 3.11.0.

On an x86_64 host, an arm64-v8a system image can be booted under the emulator's bundled QEMU, which makes SUPPORTED_ABIS[0] arm64-v8a and the app install the arm64 split. Expect a slow boot (tens of minutes) - it is not an officially supported host architecture for that image.

docs.title: The two patches
docs.text:
1. android:debuggable="true" - the app ships a network_security_config.xml containing

<debug-overrides>
    <trust-anchors><certificates src="user"/></trust-anchors>
</debug-overrides>

Android applies <debug-overrides> to every domain, but only to a debuggable app. Setting that one flag is what makes the platform trust your user-installed CA, covering the web API, CodePush and the H5 pages. Nothing on those paths pins a certificate.

2. Neutralising the MQTT certificate pin - MQTT is the exception, and it is a real pin. The app's Paho fork builds its SSLSocketFactory from a certificate embedded in a classes*.dex, loads it into an empty KeyStore, and passes that to TrustManagerFactory.init(). A non-null, app-supplied KeyStore replaces the platform trust store entirely, so <debug-overrides> and every user CA are ignored and the handshake fails with CertPathValidatorException: Trust anchor for certification path not found.

The patch keeps a prefix of that embedded string - enough for the dex's string_ids table to stay sorted, which ART verifies on every launch - and fills the rest with a marker. CertificateFactory then rejects the result, the app's factory catches the exception and returns null, and Paho builds its SSLContext with null trust managers: the platform trust store again. The result contains no reference to Bumper's CA, so it stays valid when Bumper regenerates its certificates.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Re-signing changes the app's signature. The first install replaces any existing copy and clears its data, so you will have to log in again. Keep certs/bumper-apk.jks - the script reuses it on later runs so upgrades keep your session.
  • Set APK_URL near the top of the script to patch a different app version.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
"Trust anchor for certification path not found" in logcat, robot never reacts. The MQTT pin is still in place - the app was built with SKIP_MQTT_CA=1, or with an older version of the script. Rebuild and reinstall.

The app installs but the login screen is white. The main activity crashed. Check logcat for SoLoaderDSONotFoundError; that means the device ABI does not match the split, so use an arm64 device. The script prints the ABIs it produced at the end of the build.

docker run --rm --entrypoint python3 -v "$PWD/scripts/app/apk-patch:/p:ro" \
  bumper-apk-tool /p/test-patch-mqtt-trust.py

docs.title: 🔧 Alternatives
docs.text:
Warning

These predate the script above, do not apply the MQTT patch, and are not tested against current app versions. Prefer the script above.

docs.title: 🚀 Automated script (legacy)
docs.text:
Needs: docker only, like the script above.

scripts/app/create-unpinned-app-legacy.sh runs apk-mitm in a container, which rewrites the APK so it trusts the CA you pass to it. Two differences from the latest script:

  • It embeds Bumper's CA into the app instead of relying on a user-installed one, so no certificate has to be installed on the phone - but it has to be rebuilt whenever Bumper regenerates its certificates.
  • It does not touch MQTT, so robot control will not work.

Kept because it patches differently, and is worth having when the latest script's manifest edit stops working on a future app version.

scripts/app/create-unpinned-app-legacy.sh

docs.title: 🛠️ Manual apk-mitm Method
docs.text:
Needs: node, npm, a JDK, adb, and certs/ca.crt.

This method leverages apk-mitm to patch the XAPK directly.

1. Download original XAPK:

curl -SLo ./data/eco.xapk \
  'https://d.apkpure.net/b/XAPK/com.eco.global.app?version=latest'

2. Patch with apk-mitm:

apk-mitm './data/eco.xapk' --certificate './certs/ca.crt'

3. Extract and install:

unzip -o './data/eco-patched.xapk' -d ./data/apks
adb install-multiple ./data/apks/*.apk

docs.title: 🛠️ Manual apktool Method
docs.text:
Needs: a JDK (for keytool, apksigner, java), apktool, curl, unzip, adb.

Full manual unpack, patch, and re-sign process.

1. Download and unpack:

cd ./data
APK_URL='https://d.apkpure.net/b/XAPK/com.eco.global.app?versionCode=127&nc=arm64-v8a'
APK_NAME="$(curl -sI -L "$APK_URL" | grep -o -E 'filename="[^"]+"' | cut -d'"' -f2)"
curl -SLo "$APK_NAME" "$APK_URL"
unzip "$APK_NAME" -d bump && cd bump

2. Prepare:

curl -SLo apktool.jar https://bitbucket.org/iBotPeaches/apktool/downloads/apktool_2.12.1.jar
export _JAVA_OPTIONS="-Djava.io.tmpdir=$HOME/.tmp"

3. Decode with apktool:

java -jar apktool.jar d 'com.eco.global.app.apk' --frame-path ~/.tmp/apktool-framework

4. Insert network security config:

Note

This step allows the app to trust user-installed certificates (e.g., your CA cert).

tee 'com.eco.global.app/res/xml/network_security_config.xml' > /dev/null <<'EOF'
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<network-security-config>
    <base-config cleartextTrafficPermitted="true">
        <trust-anchors>
            <certificates src="system"/>
            <certificates src="user"/>
        </trust-anchors>
    </base-config>
</network-security-config>
EOF

5. Rebuild the APK:

sed -i 's/android:gravity="0x0"/android:gravity="center"/g' com.eco.global.app/res/layout/aa30_activity_air_auto.xml
java -jar apktool.jar b 'com.eco.global.app' --frame-path ~/.tmp/apktool-framework
cp 'com.eco.global.app/dist/com.eco.global.app.apk' 'com.eco.global.app.apk'

6. Sign the APK(s):

keytool -genkey -v -keystore bumper-key.jks -alias bumper-key \
  -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000 \
  -storepass 123456 -keypass 123456 \
  -dname "CN=Bumper, OU=Bumper, O=Bumper, L=Home, S=Home, C=EU"

for apk in *.apk; do
  echo "Zipalign $apk"
  cp "$apk" "$apk.tmp"
  zipalign -p -f -v 4 "$apk.tmp" "$apk" 1>/dev/null
  rm -f "$apk.tmp"
done

for apk in *.apk; do
  echo "Signing $apk"
  apksigner sign \
    --ks bumper-key.jks \
    --ks-key-alias bumper-key \
    --ks-pass pass:123456 \
    --key-pass pass:123456 \
    --v1-signing-enabled true \
    --v2-signing-enabled true \
    --v3-signing-enabled true \
    "$apk"
done

7. Install on device:

adb install-multiple *.apk

docs.title: 🛠️ Manual android-unpinner Method
docs.text:
Needs: python3, pip/uv, a JDK, curl, unzip, adb.

Full manual unpack, patch, and re-sign process.

1. Download and unpack:

cd ./data
APK_URL='https://d.apkpure.net/b/XAPK/com.eco.global.app?versionCode=127&nc=arm64-v8a'
APK_NAME="$(curl -sI -L "$APK_URL" | grep -o -E 'filename="[^"]+"' | cut -d'"' -f2)"
curl -SLo "$APK_NAME" "$APK_URL"
unzip "$APK_NAME" -d bump && cd bump

2. Prepare:

# sudo apt install openjdk-21-jre-headless
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python3 -m pip install uv
uv tool install git+https://github.com/mitmproxy/android-unpinner
export _JAVA_OPTIONS="-Djava.io.tmpdir=$HOME/.tmp"

3. Patch APKs:

android-unpinner patch-apks *.apk
for file in *.unpinned.apk; do mv -f "$file" "${file%.unpinned.apk}.apk"; done

4. Install on device:

adb install-multiple *.apk
